rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report traces the written invocation from Quraysh’s باسمك اللهم through successive revealed forms until the full basmala was written after the verse in al-Naml.
rows.anchor: إنه من سليمان وإنه بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because every component and the complete formula occur in Qur’anic revelation, its established fame and many proofs make exclusion an attack on the reliability of the rest of the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: أجزاء هذه الكلمة كلها من القرآن ومجموعها من القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mass transmission establishes that God revealed the formula and commanded its inscription in the codex; the dispute therefore concerns legal consequences such as reciting it and touching it while impure.
rows.anchor: ثبت بالتواتر أن الله تعالى كان ينزل هذه الكلمة على محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since inclusion settles disputed ritual rules more cautiously, he favors it under the Prophetic maxim to leave doubtful matters for secure ones.
rows.anchor: ثبوت هذه الأحكام أحوط فوجب المصير إليه

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The report of prayer divided between God and the servant omits the basmala; opponents infer that it is not a verse of al-Fatiha.
rows.anchor: قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين فإذا قال العبد الحمد لله رب العالمين

rows.speaker: المخالف
rows.claim: Opponents identify the divided prayer with al-Fatiha: without the basmala its seven verses divide three-and-a-half to each side, whereas counting it gives God four-and-a-half and the servant two-and-a-half.
rows.anchor: التنصيف إنما يحصل إذا قلنا إن التسمية ليست آية من الفاتحة

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet began prayer with the takbir and recitation of al-Fatiha, which opponents take to show the basmala is not one of its verses.
rows.anchor: كان يفتتح الصلاة بالتكبير والقراءة بالحمد لله رب العالمين

rows.speaker: المخالف
rows.claim: Opponents argue that counting the basmala as a verse repeats الرحمن الرحيم within the sura, contrary to the evidence.
rows.anchor: لزم التكرار في قوله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tha‘labi transmits a version in which the Prophet counted the basmala as a complete verse of al-Fatiha; when reports conflict, affirmation outweighs omission.
rows.anchor: رواية الإثبات مقدمة على رواية النفي

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A variant transmitted by Abu Dawud al-Sijistani says God calls Malik yawm al-din a point between Himself and the servant, which supports three verses on either side when the basmala is counted.
rows.anchor: إذا قال العبد مالك يوم الدين يقول الله تعالى مجدني عبدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Half can describe a division of meaning rather than an exact count, as in calling inheritance law half of knowledge or saying half the people are angry.
rows.anchor: لفظ النصف كما يحتمل النصف في عدد الآيات فهو أيضا يحتمل النصف في المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report’s examples show that half may describe a conceptual division: inheritance law concerns the dead, while life and death are two categories; Shurayh similarly calls half the people angry when some are pleased and others displeased.
rows.anchor: الفرائض نصف العلم وسماه بالنصف من حيث أنه بحث عن أحوال الأموات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit proofs that the basmala is in al-Fatiha outweigh a report whose purpose is another point; caution also favors his position.
rows.anchor: دلائلنا في أن بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم آية من الفاتحة صريحة

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i explains Aisha’s phrase al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin as a title for the entire sura, not only its opening words.
rows.anchor: جعلت الحمد لله رب العالمين اسما لهذه السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repetition for emphasis is common in the Qur’an, and reaffirming that God is merciful is especially important.
rows.anchor: التكرار لأجل التأكيد كثير في القرآن

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: A rare report has al-Hasan al-Basri count al-Fatiha as eight verses, while the well-known view accepted by most counts seven and identifies them with the seven oft-repeated verses.
rows.anchor: في بعض الروايات الشاذة أن الحسن البصري كان يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those counting the basmala treat the final phrase from sirat alladhina through the end as one verse; Abu Hanifa, omitting the basmala, splits that ending into two verses.
rows.anchor: صراط الذين أنعمت عليهم غير المغضوب عليهم ولا الضالين آية تامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i’s count is preferable: the pause after an‘amta ‘alayhim does not match the sura’s verse endings, and verse endings elsewhere are either near-rhyming or matching.
rows.anchor: مقطع قوله صراط الذين أنعمت عليهم لا يشابه مقطع الآيات المتقدمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Starting a verse with ghayr separates a modifier or exception from what it qualifies, though each belongs syntactically with the preceding phrase.
rows.anchor: هذا اللفظ إما أن يكون صفة لما قبله أو استثناء عما قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request to guide us to the path of the blessed is incomplete without excluding those under anger or astray; the whole qualified phrase should therefore be one verse.
rows.anchor: ما لم يضم إليه قوله غير المغضوب عليهم ولا الضالين لم يصح قوله اهدنا الصراط المستقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the incomplete guidance request, al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin is a complete sentence by itself, so it can be a verse before الرحمن الرحيم.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله رب العالمين كلام تام بدون قوله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The leading authorities among al-Shafi‘i’s followers agree the basmala is Qur’an in every sura; their two opinions concern whether it is a full verse alone or joined to what follows.
rows.anchor: اتفقوا على أن بسم الله قرآن من سائر السور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Hanafis accuse al-Shafi‘i of dissenting from consensus on the basmala at every sura’s opening; Razi answers that its Qur’anic-script placement in the codex proves it is Qur’an.
rows.anchor: بسم الله مكتوب في أوائل السور بخط القرآن فوجب كونه قرآنا

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Razi opens the objection concerning basmala verse status by citing Abu Hurayra’s report about the verse count of al-Mulk.
rows.anchor: واحتج المخالف بما روى أبو هريرة أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال في سورة الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse-count objection disappears if the basmala and the words after it form one verse; a complete verse in al-Fatiha can be part of a longer verse elsewhere, and al-Kawthar’s count covers its distinctive content.
rows.anchor: إذا قلنا بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم مع ما بعده آية واحدة فهذا الإشكال زائل

rows.speaker: أحمد بن حنبل
rows.claim: Ahmad ibn Hanbal is reported to count the basmala as a verse of al-Fatiha while reciting it quietly in every rak‘a; al-Shafi‘i counts it and recites aloud, while Abu Hanifa does not count it but reads it quietly.
rows.anchor: التسمية آية من الفاتحة إلا أنه يسر بها في كل ركعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi holds loud recitation to be Sunna: if the sura is recited aloud, its opening basmala should be too, rather than making only part of a sura audible.
rows.anchor: السورة الواحدة إما أن تكون بتمامها سرية أو جهرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the basmala praises and glorifies God, making its remembrance public is fitting; the Qur’an commands abundant remembrance, as one would publicly honor a beloved father.
rows.anchor: قوله بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم لا شك أنه ثناء على الله وذكر له بالتعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Open remembrance publicly shows pride in honoring God and indifference to objection; reason commends that, supported by the reported maxim about what Muslims deem good.
rows.anchor: الجهر بذكر الله يدل على كونه مفتخرا بذلك الذكر غير مبال بإنكار من ينكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Concealment suits a defect, not the greatest honor of remembering God; reports praise dying with a tongue moist in remembrance and Ali’s saying that God’s mention ennobles those who remember Him.
rows.anchor: طوبى لمن مات ولسانه رطب من ذكر الله

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali is reported to recite the basmala aloud in all prayers, a practice Razi says strongly confirms public recitation.
rows.anchor: كان مذهبه الجهر ببسم الله الرحمن الرحيم في جميع الصلوات

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i reports that when Muawiya omitted the basmala and bowing and prostration takbirs in Medina, the Emigrants and Helpers protested and he repeated prayer with them.
rows.anchor: ثم إنه أعاد الصلاة مع التسمية والتكبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since Muawiya was powerful, the Companions’ public protest shows that aloud basmala recitation was established among them.
rows.anchor: كان كالأمر المتقرر عند كل الصحابة من المهاجرين والأنصار

rows.speaker: البيهقي
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi transmits Abu Hurayra’s report that the Prophet recited the basmala aloud, and reports the same practice from Umar, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, and Ibn al-Zubayr.
rows.anchor: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يجهر في الصلاة ببسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Razi says Ali’s loud recitation is established by mass transmission; he cites the report asking God to keep truth with Ali wherever he turns.
rows.anchor: كان يجهر بالتسمية فقد ثبت بالتواتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied verb with the basmala means beginning acts with God’s help; hearing it teaches dependence on divine protection from sin and aid for good, making its recitation a call to the best good rather than an innovation.
rows.anchor: يتعلق بفعل لا بد من إضماره والتقدير بإعانة اسم الله اشرعوا في الطاعات

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet, Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman began prayer with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin; Muslim versions say they did not mention, or were not heard saying, the basmala aloud.
rows.anchor: صليت خلف رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وخلف أبي بكر وعمر وعثمان وكانوا يستفتحون القراءة بالحمد لله رب العالمين

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن المغفل
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mughaffal says his father warned him against introducing the basmala, recalling that the Prophet and first three caliphs began with al-hamdu lillah.
rows.anchor: يا بني إياك والحدث في الإسلام فقد صليت خلف رسول الله

rows.speaker: المخالف
rows.claim: Opponents cite Qur’anic commands to invoke God humbly and remember Him inwardly as proof that the basmala should be quiet; jurists infer this from the verses and earlier reports.
rows.anchor: وبسم الله الرحمن الرحيم ذكر الله فوجب إخفاؤه

rows.speaker: أبو حامد الإسفراييني
rows.claim: Abu Hamid al-Isfarayini groups six Anas reports: three support the Hanafi position by omitting the basmala, while three contrary reports recount the protest against Muawiya, loud recitation, or Anas’s uncertainty.
rows.anchor: روي عن أنس في هذا الباب ست روايات أما الحنفية فقد رووا عنه ثلاث روايات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conflicting and unstable Anas reports leave the evidence balanced; possible Umayyad pressure against Ali’s practice may explain Anas’s hesitation, and Ali’s lifelong practice should prevail.
rows.anchor: عظم فيها الخبط والاضطراب فبقيت متعارضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If reports conflict, Razi prefers Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, and Abu Hurayra over Anas and Ibn al-Mughaffal because they were more knowledgeable and closer to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: كانوا اكثر علما وقربا من رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi invokes Abu Hanifa’s refusal of solitary reports that oppose analogy: the evident rational case favors openly reciting a phrase that honors God.
rows.anchor: خبر الواحد إذا ورد على خلاف القياس لم يقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ali, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Umar were more learned and eminent than Anas and Ibn al-Mughaffal; their likely proximity, the Prophet’s moderate voice, and gradual increase in volume explain who heard the basmala.
rows.anchor: كانوا أعلى حالا في العلم والشرف وعلو الدرجة

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i interprets Anas’s phrase that the Prophet began with al-hamdu lillah as saying al-Fatiha, named by its opening, came before other suras.
rows.anchor: أنه كان قدم هذه السورة في القراءة على غيرها من السور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mughaffal’s denial of loud recitation can mean only that the Prophet did not raise his voice excessively, as instructed by the Qur’an; an affirmative report outweighs a negative one.
rows.anchor: عدم المبالغة في رفع الصوت كما قال تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses about inward remembrance concern simple recollection; reciting God’s revealed words as worship is a different act for which audible reading is preferable.
rows.anchor: نحمل ذلك على مجرد الذكر

rows.speaker: الشيعة
rows.claim: The Shi‘a hold that the basmala should be recited aloud in both loud and quiet prayers; most jurists disagree.
rows.anchor: السنة هي الجهر بالتسمية سواء كانت في الصلاة الجهرية أو السرية

rows.speaker: المخالف
rows.claim: Those denying that the basmala is part of each sura offer two explanations for its codex placement: it separates suras, or it is Qur’an as an independent verse revealed at each opening or once for insertion throughout.
rows.anchor: اختلفوا في سبب إثباتها في المصحف في أول كل سورة وفيه قولان

rows.speaker: أم سلمة
rows.claim: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet counted the basmala as a verse marking the separation between suras.
rows.anchor: كان يعد بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم آية فاصلة

rows.speaker: عمرو بن دينار
rows.claim: Amr ibn Dinar rebukes al-Fadl al-Raqashi for claiming the basmala is not Qur’an, since it marks the end of one sura and start of another.
rows.anchor: علم أن تلك السورة قد ختمت وفتح غيرها

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن المبارك
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mubarak says omitting the basmala omits 113 verses; similar statements are attributed to Ibn Umar and Abu Hurayra.
rows.anchor: فقد ترك مائة وثلاث عشرة آية

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: For those who do not count the basmala as a verse of al-Fatiha, Abu Hanifa and several other jurists require it quietly; Malik forbids it in obligatory prayer but permits a choice in voluntary prayer.
rows.anchor: يقرأ التسمية سرا وقال مالك : لا ينبغي أن يقرأها في المكتوبة

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i’s position entails reading the basmala in every rak‘a; Abu Hanifa is reported both to require it before al-Fatiha in every rak‘a and to require it only at the start of the prayer.
rows.anchor: مذهب الشافعي يقتضي وجوب قراءتها في كل الركعات

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i prefers repeating the basmala before every sura, citing the report that an important matter begun without it is cut off.
rows.anchor: كل أمر ذي بال لا يبدأ فيه ببسم الله فهو أبتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi’s school holds that a menstruating woman or a person in major ritual impurity may not recite the basmala.
rows.anchor: والصحيح عندنا أنه لا يجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars agree that invoking God in ablution is recommended, and most do not require it because the ablution verse omits it.
rows.anchor: تسمية الله على الوضوء مندوبة وعامة العلماء على أنها غير واجبة

rows.speaker: أهل الظاهر
rows.claim: Literalists require the basmala in ablution, while Ishaq invalidates ablution for deliberate omission but excuses forgetfulness.
rows.anchor: قال أهل الظاهر إنها واجبة فلو تركها عمدا أو سهوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether meat from an animal slaughtered without the basmala is lawful is a famous dispute, with Qur’anic commands both to invoke God over offerings and not eat what was not named over.
rows.anchor: متروك التسمية عند التذكية هل يحل أكله أم لا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars recommend beginning every activity with the basmala, from sleep and waking to worship, entering and leaving home, eating, drinking, giving, and receiving; they also recommend it at birth, death, burial, resurrection, and the gathering.
rows.anchor: يستحب أن لا يشرع في عمل من الأعمال وإلا ويقول بسم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basmala at the gathering is said to distance the fire from the speaker by its blessing.
rows.anchor: فتتباعد عنه النار ببركة قوله بسم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi rejects translated Qur’an as sufficient for prayer for both able and unable reciters; Abu Hanifa allows it for either, while Abu Yusuf and Muhammad allow it only for the unable.
rows.anchor: ترجمة القرآن لا تكفي في صحة الصلاة لا في حق من يحسن القراءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi calls Abu Hanifa’s view far from sound; al-Samarqandi and al-Dabusi explicitly abandoned it.
rows.anchor: مذهب أبي حنيفة في هذه المسألة بعيد جدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet prayed using the revealed Arabic Qur’an throughout his life, so believers must follow that practice; Razi notes the irony that Abu Hanifa treats habitual head-wiping as a condition but not habitual Arabic recitation.
rows.anchor: إنما صلى بالقرآن المنزل من عند الله تعالى باللفظ العربي وواظب عليه طول عمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rightly guided caliphs prayed with Arabic Qur’an, so their practice binds believers under commands to follow Abu Bakr and Umar and the caliphs’ Sunna.
rows.anchor: أن الخلفاء الراشدين صلوا بالقرآن العربي فوجب أن يجب علينا ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet and Companions recited only Arabic in prayer; the saved group follows their practice. Muslims throughout Islamic lands agree on Arabic recitation, and departing from believers’ way is condemned.
rows.anchor: وجميع أصحابه كانوا متفقين على القراءة في الصلاة بهذا القرآن العربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer requires Qur’an recitation, and Persian words are not Qur’an: revelation is in clear Arabic, messengers speak their people’s language, and the challenge to produce its like would be contradicted if a Persian rendering counted.
rows.anchor: إن الكلام المرتب بالفارسية ليس بقرآن لوجوه

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir transmits Abu Hurayra’s report that prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening; a Persian rendering is either called Qur’an, which Razi deems ignorant and contrary to consensus, or not Qur’an.
rows.anchor: لا تجزي صلاة لا يقرأ فيها بفاتحة الكتاب

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن أبي أوفى
rows.claim: When a man could not recite Qur’an, the Prophet taught him glorification, praise, and takbir instead of a translation, showing the alternative for inability.
rows.anchor: إني لا أستطيع أن أحفظ القرآن كما يحسن في الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Qur’an could be translated as Qur’an, Christians could claim its opening was copied from the Gospel’s matching formula; no one makes that claim.
rows.anchor: أول الإنجيل هو قوله بسم إلاها رحمانا ومرحيانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Persian rendering of the cave passage or insults and requests becomes ordinary human speech, barred in prayer; the Arabic original remains distinct through its miraculous arrangement.
rows.anchor: من جنس كلام الناس لفظا ومعنى فوجب أن لا تجوز الصلاة به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If every language’s translation were Qur’an, revelation would have more than the seven canonical forms, contradicting the report that it came in seven forms.
rows.anchor: أنزل القرآن على سبعة أحرف كلها شاف كاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hanafi principle would also validate prayer with matching verses from Torah, Gospel, or ordinary writings, an outcome Razi says is alien to Islam.
rows.anchor: الصلاة صحيحة بقراءة الإنجيل والتوراة وبقراءة زيد وإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A translation of al-Fatiha reduces it to generic praise found in any sermon; allowing this would make prayer valid with all sermons, an unacceptable result.
rows.anchor: لا خطبة إلا وقد حصل فيها هذا القدر فوجب أن يقال الصلاة صحيحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If translation were permitted, the Prophet would have authorized Persians, Romans, and Ethiopians to pray in their languages; such a popular, easier permission would have spread and erased the Arabic Qur’an.
rows.anchor: قد أذن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لسلمان الفارسي في أن يقرأ القرآن بالفارسية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although a non-Arab may understand meaning more readily in translation, prayer seeks remembrance and reflection; treating translation as valid would perversely make Arabic recitation prohibited.
rows.anchor: المقصد الأقصى من إقامة الصلوات حصول هذه المعاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer preserves both meaning and Arabic wording: the wording carries the inimitable eloquence, and its required recitation safeguards memorization and fulfills God’s promise to preserve the Reminder.
rows.anchor: الإعجاز في فصاحته ؛ وفصاحته في لفظه

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Opponents cite Ibn Mas‘ud teaching an Ajami to replace al-athim with al-yatim, then saying Quranic error is replacing a mercy verse with a punishment verse rather than using a synonym.
rows.anchor: وكان الرجل عجميا فكان يقول : طعام اليتيم

rows.speaker: المخالف
rows.claim: Opponents argue that the Qur’an was in earlier scriptures, whose wording was Hebrew or Syriac rather than the Arabic wording, so meaning can be Qur’an in another language.
rows.anchor: فأخبر أن القرآن في زبر الأولين وقال تعالى

rows.speaker: المخالف
rows.claim: Opponents cite God’s statement that this Qur’an was revealed to warn people who do not understand Arabic, arguing that communicated meaning in their language is still Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وأوحي إلي هذا القرآن لأنذركم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi objects that Hanafis selectively invoke Ibn Mas‘ud: they reject his reported uncertainty about faith, though they rely on him here; reports that he omitted al-Fatiha and the protective suras likely reflect views he later abandoned.
rows.anchor: فإن كان قول ابن مسعود حجة فلم لم يقبلوا قوله في تلك المسألة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being in earlier scriptures means the Qur’an’s stories are found there, while warning people means warning them of its meaning; this limited figurative reading is warranted by decisive proofs.
rows.anchor: هذه القصص موجودة في زبر الأولين

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i’s newer view requires the follower to recite; his earlier view requires it only when the imam recites quietly, as also held by Malik and Ibn al-Mubarak, while Abu Hanifa discourages recitation behind the imam.
rows.anchor: في القول الجديد تجب القراءة على المقتدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’an 73:20 commands recitation for both a solitary worshipper and a follower behind an imam.
rows.anchor: وهذا الأمر يتناول المنفرد والمأموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet recited in prayer, so believers follow him; saying that congregational following blocks recitation merely introduces a counterargument.
rows.anchor: كان يقرأ في الصلاة فيجب علينا ذلك لقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to establish prayer includes all the Prophet’s prayer actions, including reciting al-Fatiha.
rows.anchor: أمر بمجموع الأفعال التي كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يفعلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hadith no prayer without the Opening is general; Razi says the opposing report exempting those behind an imam has been criticized.
rows.anchor: لا صلاة إلا بفاتحة الكتاب وقد ثبت تقرير وجه الدليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s instruction to a Bedouin to read whatever Qur’an is easy applies equally to the follower and the solitary worshipper.
rows.anchor: وهذا يتناول المنفرد والمأموم

rows.speaker: عبادة بن الصامت
rows.claim: A Tirmidhi report says that after worshippers admitted reading behind the imam, the Prophet told them to read Umm al-Qur’an, since prayer is invalid without it; al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عيسى الترمذي : هذا حديث حسن

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra tells a Persian worshipper to recite al-Fatiha silently even when behind an imam; Razi says this contradicts treating that prayer as deficient and supports the questioner’s understanding that recitation is required.
rows.anchor: إني أكون أحيانا خلف الإمام

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The divided-prayer report makes al-Fatiha’s recitation integral to both solitary and congregational prayer because the division occurs through recitation.
rows.anchor: بين أن التنصيف إنما يحصل بسبب القراءة

rows.speaker: عبادة بن الصامت
rows.claim: Al-Daraqutni transmits the Prophet telling followers not to recite when he reads aloud except Umm al-Qur’an, because prayer is invalid without it.
rows.anchor: لا تقرؤا شيئا من القرآن إذا جهرت بقراءتي إلا أم القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many reports promise great reward for Qur’an recitation and apply to followers, so reciting behind the imam earns reward; Razi says those accepting that reward must accept obligation.
rows.anchor: الأحاديث الكثيرة دالة على أن قراءة القرآن توجب الثواب العظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Abu Hanifa agrees recitation behind the imam does not invalidate prayer while Shafi‘i holds omission invalidates it, reciting is the safer course.
rows.anchor: القراءة خلف الإمام لا تبطل الصلاة وأما عدم قراءتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A follower unable to hear the imam would otherwise remain idle; since Qur’an recitation is the best deed, the reciter’s state is superior and therefore obligatory.
rows.anchor: أفضل الأعمال قراءة القرآن وإذا ثبت أن القراءة أفضل من السكوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If congregational following prevented recitation, following would unlawfully block a great act of worship; since following is permitted, it cannot prevent reading.
rows.anchor: لو كان الاقتداء مانعا من القراءة لكان الاقتداء حراما

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa argues from the command to listen and be quiet when Qur’an is recited; Razi says his exegesis of that verse defeats the argument, and al-Bayhaqi weakened the cited reports.
rows.anchor: في تفسير هذه الآية أنها لا تدل على قولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even assuming the opposing reports sound, Razi prefers recitation because it occupies prayer with worship, is safer, and avoids leaving time empty of remembrance.
rows.anchor: يوجب الاشتغال بقراءة القرآن وهو من أعظم الطاعات

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: The first of six positions denies that recitation is obligatory at all; this is attributed to al-Asamm and Ibn Ulayya.
rows.anchor: قول الأصم وابن علية وهو أن القراءة غير واجبة أصلا

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Hasan ibn Salih require al-Fatiha only once, reasoning that the exception in no prayer without it is fulfilled by one recitation.
rows.anchor: أن القراءة إنما تجب في ركعة واحدة لقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa requires reading in the first two rak‘as; in later ones the worshipper may read, glorify God, or remain silent, with another report requiring any two rak‘as without specifying which.
rows.anchor: القراءة في الركعتين الأولتين واجبة وهو في الأخيرتين بالخيار

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyan’s position requires reading in the first two rak‘as and regards reading in the final two as disliked.
rows.anchor: تجب القراءة في الركعتين الأوليين وتكره في الأخريين

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik requires recitation in most rak‘as: three in a four-rak‘a prayer, two in Maghrib, and both in Fajr.
rows.anchor: قول مالك أن القراءة واجبة في أكثر الركعات

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i requires recitation in every rak‘a, which Razi supports by the Prophet’s consistent practice and the command to follow him.
rows.anchor: القراءة واجبة في كل الركعات

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: The Prophet told the Bedouin to read Umm al-Qur’an and then to do likewise in every rak‘a; the command includes verbal recitation because speech is an action of the tongue.
rows.anchor: وكذلك فافعل في كل ركعة والأمر للوجوب

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sabbagh introduces Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri’s report as evidence for reciting al-Fatiha in every rak‘a; the report’s wording continues in the next segment.
rows.anchor: عن أبي سعيد الخدري أنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i’s position is said to be agreed upon by Companions including Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, and Ibn Mas‘ud.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول مجمع عليه بين الصحابة قال به أبو بكر وعمر وعلي وابن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading al-Fatiha in every rak‘a is the safer view; the standing duty remains until reciting in all units completes it fully.
rows.anchor: القراءة في الركعات أحوط فوجب القول بوجوبها

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports prayer was originally two rak‘as, retained while traveling and expanded at home; opponents infer that only the first two rak‘as are original and later ones allow lighter requirements.
rows.anchor: فرضت الصلاة في الأصل ركعتين فأقرت في السفر وزيدت في الحضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that his proofs are more numerous and stronger, and his position is more cautious.
rows.anchor: دلائلنا أكثر وأقوى ومذهبنا أحوط فكان أرجح

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i’s earlier view excuses a forgotten recitation, citing Umar’s Maghrib prayer; his newer view invalidates it because the general proofs cover both deliberate and inadvertent omission.
rows.anchor: قال الشافعي في القديم لا تفسد صلاته

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: A report says Umar omitted recitation in Maghrib and considered the prayer sound after the congregation confirmed his bowing and prostration were proper.
rows.anchor: صلى بنا عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه المغرب فترك القراءة

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i later answers the Umar report by citing al-Sha‘bi that Umar repeated the prayer, or by suggesting he omitted aloud recitation rather than recitation itself.
rows.anchor: الشعبي روى أن عمر رضي الله عنه أعاد الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recitation must follow sura order; if the latter half is read first and the first half afterward, only the first half counts.
rows.anchor: لو قرأ النصف الأخير ثم النصف الأول يحسب له الأول دون الأخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Someone who knows part of al-Fatiha reads that portion plus six other verses; one who knows no part must read whatever Qur’an they know, or glorify and praise God if they know none.
rows.anchor: إن حفظ شيئا من القرآن لزمه قراءة ذلك المحفوظ

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abu Sa‘id reports that the Messenger commanded recitation of al-Fatiha in every rak‘a, obligatory or voluntary.
rows.anchor: أمرنا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أن نقرأ فاتحة الكتاب

rows.speaker: رفاعة بن مالك
rows.claim: Rifa‘a ibn Malik reports the Prophet instructing an uninformed worshipper to praise and magnify God if he has memorized no Qur’an; for one unable to recite even Arabic remembrance, Razi recommends invoking God in any language one can manage.
rows.anchor: وإن لم يكن معه شيء من القرآن فليحمد الله وليكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the remaining case of knowing no al-Fatiha, Qur’an, or Arabic remembrance, Razi requires whatever remembrance of God is possible in any language, following the command to do as much as one can.
rows.anchor: بأي لسان قدر عليه تمسكا بقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Reports say Ibn Mas‘ud denied that al-Fatiha and the two protective suras belonged to the Qur’an, creating a dilemma for the status of transmission and his own knowledge.
rows.anchor: كان ينكر كون سورة الفاتحة من القرآن وكان ينكر كون المعوذتين من القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If transmission was mass-transmitted in the Companions’ time, Ibn Mas‘ud’s denial would imply disbelief or deficient reason; if not, Qur’an’s transmission would lack certain proof, so Razi judges the attribution false.
rows.anchor: نقل هذا المذهب عن ابن مسعود نقل كاذب باطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madḥ is broader than hamd: one may praise a living or inanimate thing such as a pearl, but cannot give it hamd.
rows.anchor: المدح قد يحصل للحي ولغير الحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madḥ can precede or follow a benefaction, whereas hamd is only after beneficence.
rows.anchor: المدح قد يكون قبل الإحسان وقد يكون بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madḥ can be condemned, as in the warning to throw dust in flatterers’ faces, whereas hamd is generally commanded.
rows.anchor: أما الحمد فإنه مأمور به مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madḥ denotes a general kind of excellence, while hamd denotes the specific virtue of benefaction; this completes the distinction that madḥ is broader.
rows.anchor: المدح عبارة عن القول الدال على كونه مختصا بنوع من أنواع الفضائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamd applies whether a benefaction reaches the speaker or someone else, while shukr is limited to a benefit received by the thankful person.
rows.anchor: الحمد يعم ما إذا وصل ذلك الإنعام إليك أو إلى غيرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying al-hamdu lillah rather than al-madhu lillah acknowledges God as a freely choosing agent, not a necessary emanation as philosophers claim.
rows.anchor: أن إله العالم ليس موجبا بالذات كما تقول الفلاسفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-hamdu lillah is better than ash-shukru lillah because it praises God for every benefit to the worlds, even one not received by the speaker; shukr is personal gratitude.
rows.anchor: كل إنعام صدر منه ووصل إلى غيره

rows.speaker: المخالف
rows.claim: One reported distinction says hamd thanks God for warding off calamity, while shukr thanks Him for gifts; an objection asks why the lesser benefit is named first.
rows.anchor: الحمد على ما دفع الله من البلاء والشكر على ما أعطى من النعماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi offers three answers: thanking for the lesser implies gratitude for the greater; warded-off harm is unbounded while gifts are finite; and preventing harm matters more than adding benefit.
rows.anchor: أنا شاكر لأدنى النعمتين فكيف لأعلاهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The formula says al-hamdu lillah rather than ahmadu Allah so it declares God worthy of praise before any creature praises Him, from eternity to eternity.
rows.anchor: كان محمودا قبل حمد الحامدين وقبل شكر الشاكرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-hamdu lillah also means praise and thanks are God’s due and property, because His abundant favors make Him inherently deserving of them.
rows.anchor: الحمد والثناء حق لله وملكه فإنه تعالى هو المستحق للحمد
